processing: Largely CTC black tea from estate factories, as is usual in Bangladesh, with some orthodox whole-leaf lots made in smaller amounts.
harvest_season: Plucked across the local growing season; no widely recognised prized flush is documented for the region.
appearance_dry: Small dark granules in CTC grades, darker twisted leaf in orthodox lots.
appearance_liquor: Deep reddish brown and full in colour, typical of strong Bangladeshi black tea.
appearance_wet: Fine, coppery-brown leaf, larger pieces in orthodox grades.
taste_profile: Described by sellers as brisk, full-bodied and malty with some sweetness, which is what you would expect from black tea of this humid valley; independent tasting notes are few.

brewing.notes: Shorter for CTC, up to four minutes for orthodox leaf. It takes milk well, which is how much of it is drunk locally.

vintage_note: Mostly reaches the market blended and without a stated year, to be drunk fresh. Occasional orthodox lots from named estates may give a season, and those are the ones worth seeking out. It is not a tea to keep and age.
description:
Sylhet is the heart of Bangladeshi tea: a humid, hilly northeastern region around the Surma Valley, where most of the country's gardens sit. Moulvibazar district has the most estates, and Sreemangal is commonly called the country's tea capital.

The tea is mainly black, and CTC is the long-standing baseline, made for a strong, quick cup. Some sellers present the region's tea as mostly orthodox whole leaf, which does not fit the wider picture of Bangladeshi production, so treat that as true of specific lots and not the region as a whole.

Expect colour and body first. Tasting notes from sellers run to brisk, malty and lightly sweet. As with other everyday black teas, it stands up to milk and sugar.

Unlike Darjeeling or Assam, Sylhet is not a protected or tightly policed name as far as is documented, so the word on a pack tells you little. A garden name is a better sign than a region alone.

If you visit, Sreemangal's tea stalls and their layered seven-colour tea are the obvious next stop.
history:
Commercial tea in the region begins at the Malnicherra estate in Sylhet, usually dated to 1854 with production from 1857, though 1849 is also given. The Surma Valley became the main centre of tea in eastern Bengal under the British, and the Assam Bengal Railway moved its crop to Chittagong for export.

The gardens continue to dominate national output, while recent coverage points to investment shortages in the local industry.
